title: Odd Times Trick the Brain
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using designer Bobby Berk's habit of setting his alarm for 5:47 instead of 5:45, this article explores how non-round, "odd" times bypass the brain's tendency to negotiate and round numbers when interpreting deadlines. Round times invite mental bargaining (snoozing to the next five-minute mark), while odd times feel deliberate and final, increasing follow-through — a phenomenon linked to the Implementation Intention Effect. The piece extends the idea to airline boarding times and how delays are perceived differently depending on whether the scheduled time was round or odd, and notes practical applications like scheduling appointments at unusual times to increase punctuality, without explicitly recommending leaders adopt the tactic themselves.
points: Round times invite mental bargaining and negotiation ("just five more minutes"); odd, non-round times feel deliberate and final.
The perceived precision of an odd time increases compliance — a pattern linked to the Implementation Intention Effect.
Airlines and other industries already exploit this: passengers treat oddly-timed flights and boarding calls as less negotiable.
A delay from a round scheduled time is perceived differently than the same delay from an odd scheduled time.
quotes: Interior Designer Bobby Berk sets his morning alarm to go off at 5:47 a.m.
Odd times interrupt the brain’s snooze-based mental math. They trick the brain into thinking differently about how much time is available.
Round numbers invite bargaining. They are mentally categorized as flexible .
The so-called Implementation Intention Effect can be used to manipulate how people view time.
The brain can play strange tricks on people, and people can purposely trick the brain. When it comes to time, it works both ways.
